prerequisites: Knowledge of algebraic calculus, trigonometry, plane and solid geometry, and the graphical representation of mathematical functions.

learning_outcomes.text: Understand the most common phenomena in nature, describe them analytically, and anticipate their evolution.
Apply the studied physical laws to solve simple problems.
Interpret the most common phenomena in nature and trace them back to the underlying physical principles.
State and demonstrate the principles of classical mechanics and the basic notions of fluids, gravitation, thermodynamics and electromagnetism.
Develop the ability to understand and describe a new phenomenon in nature, drawing inspiration from the phases of the experimental method and the logical organization of scientific theories.

syllabus_topics: Mechanics of particles and Systems: Scientific Method: Model and Experiment.
Statics and Dynamics of Rigid Bodies.
Elements of Fluid Mechanics: Fluid Statics.
Elementary microscopic interpretation of thermal phenomena.
Motion of charges subjected to the Lorentz force.
assessment_rules: The final exam consists of a written and an oral test. The written test has three exercises (two on mechanics and one on electromagnetism) to be solved in 1.5 hours. Passing the written test requires correctly solving 2 or 3 exercises (grades B or A respectively); solving 1 or 0 exercises results in a failed test (grade C). The oral test evaluates understanding of course content. The maximum final grade is 30 if the written test grade is A, and 24 if the written test grade is B. It is possible to split the final exam into two parts: one on Mechanics and one on Electromagnetism.
